To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in women with Li-Fraumenie syndrome, a rare inherited cancer predisposition syndrome, breastfeeding was found to be protective against risk of breast cancer, especially if it was at least 7 months of lifetime breastfeeding.

in this first study of breast cancer and reproductive factors in Li-Fraumenti syndrome, breastfeeding was observed as protective against breast cancer, especially with at last 7 months of breastfeeding and older age at first birth was suggestive of a slight increase in breast cancer risk.
women with Li-Fraumení syndrome, an extremely rare cancer predisposition disorder, may be more sensitive to the effects of reproductive factors than women in the general population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of risk factors for breast cancer in women who are at increased risk of developing breast cancer due to a genetic predisposition.
the role of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene, and its protein product p53, in cancer development.
the identification and validation of biomarkers for the detection of breast cancer and other diseases, and the development of novel therapeutics and imaging agents for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
breastfeeding is protective against breast cancer, but that the effect is small.
reproductive factors are not associated with breast cancer development in LFS.
reproductive factors do not significantly affect breast-cancer risk in women with LFI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
breastfeeding and older age at first birth may be associated with increased risk for breast cancer in women carrying TP53 germline mutations.
breastfeeding for 7 or more months is protective against breast cancer in women who carry germline TP 53 variants.
breastfeeding for at least seven months may be protective against breast cancers in women with Li-Fraumenie syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women with Li-Fraumenii syndrome should be counseled to breastfeed for at least 6 months, and if possible, for 12 months, as it may be a protective factor for breast cancer risk.
women with Li-Fraumenii Syndrome (LFS) may benefit from breastfeeding and delaying childbearing to reduce their breast cancer risk.
women with Li-Fraumenie Syndrome who are considering having children should be encouraged to breast feed their children for at least 6-9 months.
